603.title: The Merciful taught
603.hook: the Merciful taught the Qur'an, created the human, taught him speech (55:1–4)
603.howItsDone: Many Muslims learn the opening verses of Surah Ar-Rahman by heart; the hadith on saying what is good or staying silent is often taught as a rule for everyday speech.

segments.voice: Yesterday: dhikr, the chorus of Surah Al-Qamar, and your line, is there any who will remember? Today, a new surah.

A toddler points at a dog and says a first word. Everyone in the kitchen stops. Someone grabs a phone to film it. Nobody claps when a child first breathes on their own, or first digests a meal, but a first word gets a whole room cheering. Surah fifty-five opens with no oath and no mysterious letters. It opens with one word, a name of God: Ar-Rahman, the Merciful. And the first things it says the Merciful did are about teaching, and about speech.

Pickthall's first four verses: "The Beneficent / Hath made known the Qur'an. / He hath created man. / He hath taught him utterance." In Arabic, four short beats: Ar-Rahman. 'Allamal-Qur'an. Khalaqal-insan. 'Allamahul-bayan. Notice the order: teaching the Qur'an comes before creating the human. Commentators have turned that over. Some read it as rank: guidance is named first as the greatest of the gifts that follow. Others note the surah is a list of mercies, and the Qur'an is named before the one who receives it. Then what the human was taught: al-bayan, from the root b-y-n, to be clear, to stand apart. Bayan is more than making sounds. It's speech that makes something plain, that lets what's inside one person become clear to another. Commentators give it wide range: speech itself, the ability to explain, the power to tell good from bad and say why. And all of it sits under the name Ar-Rahman. The surah frames speech as mercy. If it's a mercy, how it's used matters. A hadith in Bukhari puts it in one line: the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ said that whoever believes in God and the Last Day should say what is good, or stay silent. The same gift that names a dog in a kitchen can also wound, flatter or lie. The surah treats it as something given; the hadith, as something you answer for.

604.title: The balance
604.hook: He set the balance, so don't transgress it: weigh justly (55:7–9)
604.howItsDone: Islamic law has long treated honest weights and measures as a religious duty; historically a market inspector, the muhtasib, checked traders' scales, and these verses of Ar-Rahman are quoted as a reminder of fair dealing.

segments.voice: Yesterday: bayan, clear speech, a gift from the Merciful, and your line, taught to speak.

At a market stall, a woman scoops lentils onto an old brass scale. The pan dips; she adds a pinch, takes a pinch away, and waits until the needle sits dead center. The customer watches the needle, not her face. Both know how easy it would be to lean a thumb on the pan. Surah Ar-Rahman, a few verses after speech, lifts its eyes to the whole sky. Then, in the same breath, it comes straight back down to that scale.
screen: `A BRASS SCALE AT A MARKET STALL.`

segments.voice: Verses seven to nine. Pickthall: "And the sky He hath uplifted; and He hath set the measure, That ye exceed not the measure, But observe the measure strictly, nor fall short thereof." Pickthall says measure; the Arabic is mizan, three times in three short verses. Mizan comes from the root w-z-n, to weigh: a balance, a pair of scales. Look at what sits side by side: a sky raised high, and a balance set down. Commentators read the first mizan as the order God built into creation, everything in proportion. Then the next two verses turn it into a command for people. Don't transgress in the balance. Set up the weight with justice, and don't make the balance short. The cosmic order and the shopkeeper's scale are the same word. Cheating at a scale isn't small in this picture; it's a crack in the order that holds up the sky. The Qur'an returns to this elsewhere. Surah Al-Mutaffifin opens with woe to those who take full measure for themselves and give short measure to others. The prophet Shu'ayb told his people again and again to give full measure and weight. And the Mizan has one more meaning. On the Day of Judgment, the Qur'an says, God will set up just scales, and no soul will be wronged in the least. So the word stretches from the stars, to the market, to the last day: one balance, kept fair at every size.
screen: `MIZAN: FROM W-Z-N, TO WEIGH.` · `THE SKY RAISED, THE BALANCE SET.` · `DON'T MAKE THE BALANCE SHORT.` · `JUST SCALES ON THE LAST DAY.`

segments.voice: Let your breath even out, in and out the same length, like two pans settling. Then think of one place where a scale tips your way a little, work you claim, time you take, praise you hand out unevenly, and picture setting the needle back to center.
Mizan. The balance, from the root to weigh: the order of creation, the honest scale, and the just scales of the last day. Today's word.
Your line: keep the balance. One word spans the sky and the market scale. That's day six hundred four.

605.title: Which favors will you deny?
605.hook: the refrain repeated thirty-one times: which of your Lord's favors will you deny (55:13)
605.howItsDone: Surah Ar-Rahman is often recited aloud, and some Muslims, hearing the refrain, quietly answer that they deny none of their Lord's favors, following the report in Tirmidhi.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the mizan, one balance from the sky to the market, and your line, keep the balance.

The Prophet ﷺ once recited a whole surah to his companions, a report in Tirmidhi says, and they listened to the end in silence. Then he told them another audience had answered it better. Not with silence: with words, every time a certain line came round. And it came round a lot. In Surah Ar-Rahman, one question returns again and again, after fruit, after the seas, after the rising places of the sun. Today, that question, and who answered it.

Verse thirteen, the first of thirty-one times it appears. Pickthall: "Which is it, of the favours of your Lord, that ye deny?" In Arabic: fa-bi-ayyi ala'i rabbikuma tukadhdhiban. Two things hide in the grammar. First, rabbikuma, your Lord, and tukadhdhiban, you deny, are dual: they speak to two. Verse thirty-three addresses the company of jinn and humans, and commentators read the whole refrain as spoken to both. Second, ala'. Pickthall says favors, the usual reading: blessings, bounties, gifts. Some commentators add that ala' can also carry the sense of wonders, signs of power. So the line asks which of these gifts, and which of these marvels, will you call a lie? Notice it's a question, not an accusation. The surah lists a gift, then stops and asks. Fruit and palm trees: which will you deny? The two seas and their pearls: which will you deny? Even warnings get the refrain, as if being warned were a kindness too. Now the report. The better audience, the Prophet told his companions, was the jinn. Each time he reached the refrain, they replied that they denied none of their Lord's favors, and praise belonged to Him. Some listeners still answer the refrain that way under their breath. On this reading, the repetition isn't filler. It's a stop after every blessing, long enough to notice it.
screen: `FA-BI-AYYI ALA'I RABBIKUMA.` · `SPOKEN TO TWO: JINN AND HUMANS.` · `A QUESTION, NOT AN ACCUSATION.` · `THE JINN ANSWERED IT.`

segments.voice: Let one ordinary gift come to mind, the breath you're taking, the light in the room, someone who texted you this week, and ask quietly: which of His favors? If you pray, answer as the report says the jinn did, that you deny none of them; if not, simply name the gift and move to the next.

Your line: which of his favors? The refrain is a pause after every gift. Day six hundred five, done.

606.title: Two seas
606.hook: two seas meet with a barrier between them they don't cross (55:19–20)
606.howItsDone: Muslims recite these verses of Ar-Rahman as signs of God's order in nature; the word barzakh is also widely known as the name for the state between death and resurrection.

segments.voice: Yesterday: ala', the favors the refrain asks whether you'll deny. Your line was which of his favors?

Stand on a bridge where a muddy river runs into clear water, and sometimes you can see the line: brown on one side, blue-green on the other, running side by side before they blend. Pour cream into cold coffee without stirring and you get a small version on the kitchen table. Two things touching, not mixing yet. Surah Ar-Rahman, among its gifts, points at exactly this: water meeting water, and something in between that holds them apart.

Verses nineteen and twenty. Pickthall: "He hath loosed the two seas. They meet. There is a barrier between them. They encroach not." The word for barrier is barzakh. It's a rare word, and it travels. In Surah Al-Furqan, the Qur'an pictures the same scene: one sea sweet and fresh, the other salt and bitter, with a barzakh between them. In Surah Al-Mu'minun, barzakh names something else: the barrier behind the dead, the in-between state from death until the resurrection. So the word means a boundary that separates two things without either disappearing. Then: from both of them come pearls and coral, and after that, the refrain: which of your Lord's favors will you deny? The two seas aren't a problem to fix. Both are gifts, and both bring up treasure. How to picture it? Classical commentators thought of fresh rivers flowing into the salt sea, or of the seas of the earth and the sky. In modern times, some writers connect the verse to estuaries and to layers of water with different saltiness that mix only slowly. Others caution against tying a verse to any one finding. The Qur'an presents the two seas as a sign, something to notice, not a lab report. What everyone can take from it is the shape: two things meet, a limit holds, and each keeps what it is while both give something precious.
screen: `TWO SEAS LOOSED. THEY MEET.` · `BARZAKH: A BARRIER BETWEEN.` · `PEARLS AND CORAL FROM BOTH.` · `A SIGN TO NOTICE.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes and see a wide river mouth, brown fresh water rolling out, the open sea coming in, and find the line where they meet. Breathe in and feel the river push out; breathe out and feel the sea hold its place, neither side winning. If a relationship or a choice of yours sits on a line like that, let it rest there too.
Two seas. Surah Ar-Rahman says two seas meet with a barzakh between them, and both bring up pearls and coral. Today's word.

607.title: Everything perishes but His face
607.hook: all on earth passes, and the face of your Lord remains, full of majesty and honor (55:26–27)
607.howItsDone: Many Muslims say a short remembrance after the obligatory prayer that ends with 'Possessor of Majesty and Honor', following the hadith in Sahih Muslim.

segments.voice: Yesterday: two seas, meeting with a barzakh between them, and your line, two seas, one barrier. Today closes Surah Ar-Rahman.

Open the photos on your phone and scroll back ten years. The café in that picture closed. The dog is gone. The friend in the corner moved across the world. Even the phone that took it is in a drawer somewhere, dead. Nothing stayed as it was, not even the light. In the middle of all its gifts, Surah Ar-Rahman says this out loud, in two short verses. Then it names the one thing it says does not pass.
screen: `THE CAFÉ CLOSED. THE DOG IS GONE.`

segments.voice: Verses twenty-six and twenty-seven. Pickthall: "Everyone that is thereon will pass away; There remaineth but the Countenance of thy Lord of Might and Glory." In Arabic: kullu man 'alayha fan, wa yabqa wajhu rabbika dhul-jalali wal-ikram. Fan means passing away; yabqa, remains. Two verbs, set against each other. And the one who remains is described with a phrase that comes back in daily prayer: dhul-jalali wal-ikram, Possessor of Majesty and Honor. A hadith in Muslim records that on finishing the prayer, the Prophet ﷺ would say a short line ending: blessed are You, Possessor of Majesty and Honor. So this verse's phrase lives in the routine of prayer. What does face mean here? Muslims have answered in more than one way. Some Sunni theologians affirm the face as an attribute of God, real but unlike anything created, without asking how. Others read face as God's very self, his essence. And some commentators add a third layer: what remains is whatever was done for God's face, for his sake. Surah Al-Qasas uses the same word: everything perishes except his face. Now notice where the verses sit. Right after them comes the refrain: which of your Lord's favors will you deny? Passing away is listed among the favors. Commentators explain it in different ways, but one reading is this: if everything here lasted forever, nothing would point beyond itself. Because things pass, they make room to notice what stays.
screen: `FAN: PASSING. YABQA: REMAINS.` · `POSSESSOR OF MAJESTY AND HONOR.` · `WHAT FACE MEANS: MORE THAN ONE READING.` · `PASSING AWAY, LISTED AS A FAVOR.`

segments.voice: Pick up something near you, a cup of tea going cold, a pen running low, or just your own open hand, and hold it lightly, knowing it won't last, without gripping harder. If you pray, you can say quietly, ya dhal-jalali wal-ikram, O Possessor of Majesty and Honor, the words from the hadith; if not, simply hold it and breathe.

Your line: his face remains. Passing away, too, is listed among the favors. That's day six hundred seven.

608.title: Three kinds of people
608.hook: on that Day, the companions of the right, of the left, and the foremost (56:7–10)
608.howItsDone: Some Muslims recite Surah Al-Waqi'ah regularly, often in the evening; its picture of the three groups is often taught alongside the verses about receiving one's record in the right or left hand.

segments.voice: Yesterday closed Surah Ar-Rahman: wajh, the face that remains, and your line, his face remains.

Surah fifty-six doesn't ease you in. Its first word is a when: when the event befalls. Al-Waqi'ah, the thing that happens, the event that cannot be avoided. Then the pictures: no one can deny its coming, it lowers some and raises others, the earth is shaken, the mountains crumble to scattered dust. Everything people stand on gives way. And in all that noise, the surah does something very calm. It sorts humanity into three groups.

Verse seven. Pickthall: "And ye will be three kinds." First, ashab al-maymanah, those on the right hand. Second, ashab al-mash'amah, those on the left hand. Third, as-sabiqun, the foremost. Notice the form of the first two. The verse names the group, then asks about it: those on the right hand, what of those on the right hand? Commentators hear it as: you can't begin to imagine. Left and right aren't random. The Qur'an elsewhere describes people receiving the record of their deeds on the Day: one given it in the right hand, glad and calling out, read my book; another given it in the left, wishing it had never been handed over. Commentators connect the companions of the right to those whose record comes in the right hand. And maymanah shares its root with yumn, blessing and good fortune, while mash'amah is tied to shu'm, ill omen. Then the surah describes each group. The right hand gets thornless lote trees, spreading shade, water flowing. The left gets scorching wind and shadowless smoke. And the foremost get a place near to God, which is tomorrow's verse. Notice the size of the frame. In one verse, everyone is sorted into just three kinds. Not by tribe, wealth or language, but by what they did and how they turned. The surah doesn't say which you are. It lays out the three and leaves you to look.
screen: `YE WILL BE THREE KINDS.` · `THE RIGHT HAND, THE LEFT HAND.` · `YUMN: BLESSING. SHU'M: ILL OMEN.` · `NOT BY TRIBE OR WEALTH.`

609.title: The foremost
609.hook: the foremost in faith will be foremost that Day, the ones brought near (56:10–11)
609.tomorrow: The water you drink, the fire you light
609.howItsDone: Muslims are encouraged to begin the greeting of salam and to hurry to the prayer and to good deeds; the foremost of these verses are often described as those who are first to good.

segments.voice: Yesterday: maymanah, the right hand, among Al-Waqi'ah's three groups. Your line was three groups. Today, the third.

A school sports day, the first race about to start. A row of kids, toes on the line, and one already leaning forward before the whistle. Whatever happens at the finish, that's the one who wanted to go. Surah Al-Waqi'ah has just named the people on the right and the people on the left. Then it names a third group, and says their name twice, like a starter calling it over the crowd.

Verses ten and eleven. Pickthall: "And the foremost in the race, the foremost in the race: Those are they who will be brought nigh." In Arabic: was-sabiquna s-sabiqun, ula'ika l-muqarrabun. Commentators read the doubling two ways. The foremost here are the foremost there: first to good in this life, first on that Day. Or simply: the foremost, and what foremost they are. Who are they? Early commentators gave many answers, and they fit together: the first to believe in every prophet's time; the first to the prayer when the call is made; the first to repent; the first to do good. Their reward is a word, muqarrabun, the ones brought near. Near to God. The next verses add a surprise: a multitude of those of old, and a few of those of later times. Commentators differ on who those are. The Qur'an asks for this eagerness elsewhere too. Surah Al-Baqarah says: vie with one another in good works. Not compete to beat someone; compete to reach the good first. And the hadith brings it down to the smallest thing. Bukhari records that the Prophet ﷺ spoke of two people who'd fallen out and stopped speaking; the better of the two, he said, is the one who greets first. So being foremost can be as small as saying salam before the other person does.
screen: `THE FOREMOST, THE FOREMOST.` · `MUQARRABUN: BROUGHT NEAR.` · `MANY OF OLD, FEW OF LATER TIMES.` · `THE BETTER ONE GREETS FIRST.`

segments.voice: Picture the first few people you'll see after this, someone at home, a coworker, the person at the counter, and imagine catching one's eye and saying hello first, warmly; if you're Muslim, that may be as-salamu alaykum. If there's someone you've been avoiding, picture them too, and the first word you might say.
The foremost. As-sabiqun, those first to good in this life, said twice, and called the ones brought near. Today's word.
Your line: first in good. The week ran from Ar-Rahman's balance, refrain, two seas and his face to Al-Waqi'ah's three groups and its foremost. See you tomorrow.

original.note: Arabic: and the foremost, the foremost. From s-b-q, to go ahead, to win a race.

trapdoor: what you thought: the foremost are the most famous believers.
what it means: those first to good here, brought near there; many of the earlier, few of the later.
what a scholar hears: the doubling is read as 'foremost here, foremost there' or as emphasis; 56:13–14 says many of the earlier and few of the later; muqarrabun from q-r-b, nearness.

chat.says: Who are 'the foremost' in Surah Al-Waqi'ah?
options: Those first to good, like the first to pray or repent; they're brought near.
The first people ever born, who lived closest in time to Adam.
Those who beat others in this life to wealth and success.
chat.meaning: Early commentators: the first to believe, to pray, to repent, to do good. 56:11 calls them muqarrabun, the ones brought near.
